To suggest for a moment that he has a mandate to do so is foolish, as the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) so ably pointed out. We were a little disappointed he was not with us last evening to back up his able presentation.
This is the general feeling across Canada now. I should like to quote for a moment from the Victoria Daily Colonist with regard to the stubbornness of the Prime Minister in pursuing his present policy and trying to force this flag down our throats, in dividing Canada and forcing a division which, if he continues, may take years to heal. The editorial has this to say:
Where does the blame for the present parliamentary stalemate lie? Solely in Mr. Pearson's obduracy over the flag issue. This is the core that keeps parliament sitting and the normal business of the country held back from speedy progression.
This has been evident ever since he introduced the flag resolution. To begin with he held the threat of an election over M.P.s' heads did they fail to pass the flag measure, which was tantamount to holding a gun at their heads and depriving them of unbiased decision.
I want to say a word a little later with regard to the free vote which we saw last evening.
He refused a free vote on the subject. While blaming Mr. Diefenbaker for non-compliance he has now prevented the compromise suggestion that would delay the contentious flag bill to a fall session by insisting on an unacceptable time limit to its debate.
It is not so much the question of the time limit that is unacceptable. It is this flag which is unacceptable to a majority of Canadians and we as Conservatives have to see that it is never unfurled on a public standard in Canada, period. There is no other attitude we can take. The editorial continues:
It is not obstructionism on the part of Mr. Diefenbaker that is at fault but the Prime Minister's insistence on having his own way. Mr. Pearson says he is not prepared to call an election on any of the current issues facing parliament, the flag of course being the main one. Is he afraid of the result?

I say he is.
This would probably be the quickest and most salutary solution to a parliamentary stalemate that grows worse with each passing day.
I too say that if he is going to insist on trying to force this flag upon us then let him call an election. Let him call an election on this issue. I do not particularly care for another election but if he is going to insist on pushing this bunting down our throats at a time when national unity in Canada is precarious, if he insists on choosing this time to push his flag upon us, then surely he must face the consequences. As I said initially, he cannot substitute stubbornness for statesmanship. He should ask the people. If he does not want an election then let him ask the people through a plebiscite, and so that we will create unity let us not have the results announced provincially. Let the results be announced on a countrywide basis. Let us keep it ultra secret. We cannot rely upon the responsibility of the press in this matter because the press of Canada has shown itself in the main to be completely irreponsible.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: You have just read from the press.
That was a private article and I only read it because I agree with it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: There are two kinds of press.

I will have a few more words to say about the press and particularly with regard to the editorial which was quoted by my colleague, the hon. member for Edmoton East (Mr. Skoreyko). I want to say a few words with regard to the editorial in the Edmonton Journal particularly because we in northern Alberta are faced with a monopoly situation. It is the only newspaper and it is thrust down our throats somewhat like Mr. Pearson's pennant. We have got to accept it whether we like it or not.
When the flag issue was first raised this newspaper was against replacing the union jack or red ensign. They wrote editorials saying it was a shame that we were going to have to go to Honolulu to look at the union jack. I do not know whether their conscience is troubling them, but now they are writing editorials saying that we should get it over with, and advocating closure. I wonder whether the publisher is not just covering up for himself or did he get a phone call from somebody else in the Southam organization, which seems to be in the hands of the Liberal party? The hon. member for York-

Humber outlined some of the benefits that can come from supporting your party at the right time. Was the Southam organization told there would be no more senatorships unless they fell into line? Was it a case like that of Maclean's, which got rid of its editor and Ottawa correspondent without a murmur from their friends in the journalistic profession? They allowed these men to be scalped without one of them having enough gumption to stand up and protect them. They talk about freedom of the press: They are using it now to cover up their own inadequacies.
On the subject of national unity and the manner in which the government has brought in this flag I want to quote rather extensively from an article in the Winnipeg Free Press of August 31 last written by no less a person than Mr. Peter Newman. We who have been here over the past few years have a good knowledge of Mr. Newman's writings. Some of them we did not like because he was a bit inaccurate, but some we had to accept. However, he has a very interesting view with regard to the flag situation and I think it is worth while to put some of his comments on the record. He is talking about the fact that the Prime Minister wanted to become a hero out of the flag debate and the main theme of his article is that the hero of the flag debate may now become the victim. I have to admit that Mr. Newman may be slightly biased because he wrote that the present government was a grey, dismal failure, and he was fired or was told he could not write such things. I am not sure which. In any event, he had the courage of his convictions and wrote what he felt about it, even though it cost him his job. As I say, he may be a little bit upset. He may still feel that any way we can get rid of this dismal grey failure of a government would be worth while. In any event, he goes on talking about the hero of the flag who may become the victim, and I quote:
But when the actual flag resolution was tabled by Pearson in the Commons it turned out to be a piece of legislative whimsy that defied the laws of political gravity. Instead of being the only major nation in the world without its own distinctive flag, we were urged to perpetuate our unique position by becoming the only land on the earth's surface to fly two official flags. Once again, Lester Pearson had tried to square the circle of political leadership.
This double-barrelled flag resolution apparently grew out of the insistence-
I am sorry the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) is not here.
-of Jack Pickersgill, who first articulated the idea at a little-reported young Liberal rally in Quebec city on February 2, 1962. Pickersgill suggested then that Canada should have one flag
Canadian Flag
to represent the commonwealth connection as well as a distinctive flag of its own and pointed out that there's no reason "why Canada can't have two official flags just as she has two official languages."
We are talking about national unity and those are the views of the Minister of Transport. The article continues as follows:
As Newfoundland's chief representative in the federal Liberal hierarchy, Pickersgill in turn was under pressure from Premier Joey Smallwood, who fears that a new flag would become the focal point of anti-Canadian feeling on this island.
In retrospect, it's clear that Pearson's two-flag resolution was a political miscalculation of major proportions.
Then, I wanted to put on the record what this writer has to say with regard to the question of a filibuster, if you can call it that. I quote:
The Conservatives' filibuster has not (as is generally believed) prevented parliament from dealing with a backlog of essential legislation. The Liberal administration, unaccountably, has no major bills ready for debate.
Is this flag debate being forced upon us because the Liberal cabinet does not have legislation ready for debate? Is this why we are debating the flag? I think some members on the front benches should have something to say with regard to that.
The pension plan, which was supposed to be the showpiece of the Liberals' first year in office is now in its fourth, sad mutation.
But the Tory filibuster has succeeded in softening Pearson's stand. He has retreated on his pledge (repeated as late as June 18) that his government would fall with the rejection of his flag.
Then he goes on to talk about the proposed alternatives that are available to the Prime Minister, and I think they are worthy of consideration. I quote:
The Liberal leader now must choose between three alternatives: He can ram his flag design through the Commons by using closure and thereby provide Diefenbaker with a natural election issue; he can allow the flag to go before a parliamentary committee, which might delay a decision indefinitely or force on him a compromise design which he could not accept; or he can let the Tory filibuster continue and hope that public revulsion with Diefenbaker's tactics will force a Conservative retreat.
Let me say here and now that we do not intend to retreat because we represent the majority of the people in Canada. As pointed out so ably by the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan), Mr. Newman ends his article in this way:
It's a grim choice, but Pearson isn't discouraged. "Every good flag has to be bom in battle," he told a friend recently, "and this one is no exception."

Canadian Flag
Are we having this flag debate so that Liberal ministers may get their legislation ready, and so that we can cover up their faults? Is this the reason we are discussing this emotional issue which may divide this country? Is this government going to continue to perpetuate the division in Canada? How much better it would be if we were to have national unity in Canada and get on with the business before the house, get on with legislation which would bring about improved economic opportunities and improved economic returns to the people. If we do not improve the standards of living in some areas of Canada, how are we going to get unity? We are not going to achieve it through a flag. We are going to get unity in Canada by improving the standards of living of some areas so that there will be equality right across this country. This was the task we of the official opposition set ourselves at a time when we formed the government, and we took many steps toward this goal. This is what this government should be doing now, instead of forcing an emotional issue upon the people of this country and furthering disunity.
How much better it would be if, for instance, the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury), were discussing legislation to improve the standard of living in some areas of Canada, instead of reading the newspaper this afternoon. How much better it would be if we were discusing legislation which would increase the economic opportunities of all Canadians. Are we discussing the flag because the minister has not done his homework and has not got legislation ready? I understand he has many $10,000 a year men in his department. Let them get busy and draft some legislation to be introduced in this house which will do something to bring about unity in Canada and to improve the standard of living of our people. We have a big job to do.
How much better it would be if we were spending our time listening to the minister of northern affairs introduce legislation to solve the problems of our north country. He is quoted enthusiastically by correspondents about what should be done in our north. So far, we have heard nothing but words. We want to see some action from this so-called decisive government. We have not heard a decision yet except the stubborn refusal of the Prime Minister to do anything except consider the flag, even if it divides this country for years to come. No one said there was anything wrong with the old one. Even the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. 
Caouette) said they did not care what kind of flag we had in the west of Canada because they had their own flag. Obviously, the Prime Minister wanted it to go through, and this is clear if one reads Mr. Lynch's report. This is the Prime Minister's personal touch; he wants this moment of glory. However he is now heading down the road toward becoming the victim of his own glorious notion. I think the people of Canada should have an improved standard of living, and then we could come together under one flag that would be acceptable to all the people of this country.
But oh no, we are going to be forced to go on and, as the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Skoreyko) said, this is just a start. This is the first of the bipartite flag resolution. Then we have to go on to the bipartite anthem resolution. Is the Prime Minister going to keep us here for the next year deciding on a symbol? Let us get on with the work that is to be done. Let us make ARDA a living thing. Let it not die, as the government is trying to let it. There is work to be done even in Alberta, in ARDA. There is work to be done in Quebec. These are things which will bring unity.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I hesitate to interrupt the hon. member. I realize some of his remarks are related to the subamendment, but when he discusses such things as ARDA in Alberta he is straying some distance away from the subject matter before the house.

Well, Your Honour, I am just pointing out that the subamendment calls for a provision which will create unity in Canada. Goodness knows, we need something. With the government we have in office we need anything we can get if we are to perpetuate unity in this country. I am merely pointing out that rather than have the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) sitting here reading his mail and the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) reading the paper, they could be doing concrete things. We in western Canada are waiting for the Minister of Agriculture to bring in his farm machinery bill. That is one of the things we want to get on with.
The farmers are waiting too.
Let's go then, my hon. friend.
Let's vote then.

We are not
going to allow the party in power to push this flag on the Canadian people, because it does not have a mandate to do it and, as I

said a moment ago, we represent the majority thought at the moment in Canada on the flag issue.
With regard to the plebiscite and the issuing of federal results, I would point out that the Prime Minister and his cabinet, like all good politicians, are a little bit egotistical. They said this is what we were elected for, to decide a flag for Canada. I dispute that. Many politicians I know are a little bit egotistical. Most politicians get here because they are leaders in some parts of their communities or constituencies, but not for a moment does this mean they have the ability to decide on an emotional question such as the flag. What about all the other people who feel they do not have that political bent but are concerned emotionally about the flag. Are we going to refuse them an opportunity to express their views about a symbol such as the flag? This is something that should be settled by a plebiscite, but I do not agree there are very many other things that should be settled that way.
We were elected to run the country as members of parliament. We were not elected to settle the question of an emotional symbolism. As I said before, we were elected to get on with the job of improving the economic situation in Canada, of providing defence, of passing legislation with regard to taxes, and we have had some evidence from the government of how it can do that. We are charged with the job of making Canada run. We are not charged nor are we suitably equipped to pick an emotional symbol for Canada. X do not believe politicians are emotionally equipped to pick an emotional symbol. We have already seen evidence of this.
At first the Prime Minister said it would be a free vote and each member would be allowed to vote as his conscience dictated. Then he said his government would stand or fall on the result, and the other day he reversed his position and said there would be a free vote, but by that time it was far too late. This is the very reason why politicians cannot decide the flag. Last night we saw that all those people on the government backbenches who were opposed to the government stand did not vote. So, it became an emotional issue and this emotional issue is decided on a political basis. Therefore instead of a national flag we have a political party flag. This is what happens if you allow politicians to decide a flag. It is going to be decided on the basis of political party lines and, as the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) said, "You either vote the party
Canadian Flag
line or you don't get into the Senate". I leave that for your consideration.
I wish to quote from the Toronto Telegram of August 22 on the question of a free vote:
At this stage, with party lines hardened, it is difficult to conceive of a truly free vote.
Having shown, belatedly, a willingness to retreat from his earlier stubborn demands for the banner of his choice, he now should go one step further and measure public sentiment by plebiscite.
Perhaps Mr. Pearson fears the outcome of such a testing of public opinion.
That is my opinion, that he fears the outcome of a plebiscite as much as he fears an election. It is my opinion he should have one or the other, dissolve the house and call an election on the flag issue, or present it to the people in the form of a plebiscite.
There is no reason why this obstructive and divisive bill should not be shelved pending a reference to the people. There is no urgency. Most Canadians outside Quebec appear to be quite satisfied with the flag we have now. In Quebec, the matter is of little importance as there they fly the Laurentian flag with its white cross and fleur-de-lis.
Until Mr. Pearson softens his stand, the opposition is justified in continuing a modified filibuster. As distasteful as such devices are in parliament, no other method seems practical in the face of Mr. Pearson's stubbornness.
The way out of the parliamentary impasse is clear: a plebiscite to end the long debate and to allow parliament to get on with more important legislation.
With regard to the Prime Minister causing disunity in Canada, I want to say he has even caused disunity in some of our minor parties. The Social Credit league of Alberta passed a resolution endorsing the maintenance of the red ensign as Canada's national flag. People in Alberta are quite satisfied with the red ensign. Most of them would be quite satisfied with a modification of that ensign to denote the history of Canada, so eloquently outlined this afternoon by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill). But most of all people in Alberta are anxious about the government, about its stubborn refusal to get on with the business of Canada. We come from a country out there where we believe there are many things to do, many opportunities for our people, and to get some of these opportunities going we need government direction. We are not getting it from this government. Fortunately the last government which was in power did something. We did get some direction. We are still seeing the benefits of it out there.
Recently the minister of northern affairs went to drive the silver spike at the Northwest Territories boundary of the Great Slave Lake Railway. I wonder why the Minister of

Canadian Flag
Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) did not go. We sat in this house and watched him vote against the construction of this railway. Now his colleagues have a big delegation to drive in the silver spike. If they really want to name this railway properly, they should call it the Baldwin-Bigg railway for northern Alberta. Here was an example of unity, an example of compromise in order to prevent a split in a certain section of this country. I think this could serve as an example to members of this house, particularly on the government side, with regard to the matter now before us. Here were two members, each representing half of the northern part of a province. A railway was proposed to go through one of these areas. By their ability and statesmanship, these members were able to accept one another's points of view and got this railway going into the north country, leaving aside all pettiness and questions of personal betterment so as to enable the building of this railway to begin. This is a real example of what the government should be doing with regard to these things.
If we raise the standard of living by providing opportunities for all Canadians-I come back to this theme-we shall have unity in this country. If the standard of living is raised to an equal level for all our people we shall have no trouble in finding a symbol. By the time we have done that, as a result of advances in education and communications, we shall be able to sit down and find a symbol which will be acceptable to the whole of this nation.
In conclusion may I repeat that the government owes it to the people of Canada to suspend this debate, to put this resolution back where they have put three or four of them in the past-they have a place for these things-and leave it there until the time comes when there is such unity in Canada that we can have a single flag which will suit everybody. Let us get on with the legislation of the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury). Let us put some of his $10,000 a year boys to work on contributing directly to the prosperity of this nation. At the same time, we do not intend to submit to the pressure now being applied. We shall not allow this bunting to be unfurled in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, in rising once again in this discussion, I want to say right away that I have no apologies to offer for doing so, because I think I would be remiss as a member of the

house not to air my views as well as those of my constituents.
It is generally admitted, Mr. Speaker, that the way in which the flag issue was introduced in the house roused a whole gamut of protests throughout Canada which can only result in a threat to Canadian unity. Now, it is with this thought in mind and the idea of doing something to strengthen Canadian unity that I rise this afternoon to explain my position.
I would like first of all to repeat that freedom of action and thought, which is our privilege in this party, entitles me to repeat that I favour a distinctive national flag. Yesterday's events, Mr. Speaker, proved that freedom of action and a free vote only exist on this side of the house. I cannot dwell on this matter, but may I point out the clearly established fact that we of the Conservative party are fully free with regard to the national flag as well as to all other matters submitted to us, and if we come back to the subject, it is because we believe that it is our duty to do so. I would like to ask hon. members opposite, who are so talkative outside the House of Commons, to seize this opportunity of submitting to the house the views of the people who sent them here.
Mr. Speaker, I must say again that the situation has not changed at all since the resolution on both flags was before us. By the way, I want to mention first that we on this side of the house, the members of the official opposition, support one flag, and not two as provided by the resolution now before us.
It is clear that the Conservative party has been supporting a distinctive national flag for many years. I want to repeat before the house that we want only one national flag, and not two flags, with one borrowed from a foreign nation.
Mr. Speaker, since we are dealing with the plebiscite question, I should like to call the attention of the house to the result of a poll I made in my riding-I say a poll, but to be more accurate, I should say two polls, because I carried out two-during the month of May, when we heard that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) would introduce a resolution concerning two flags. I immediately contacted my constituents to know exactly the viewpoint of those I represent here. On May 22, 1964, I sent 1,600 questionnaires to the people in my riding, who represent all classes of society. Here are those questions:
Are you in favour of keeping the Canadian red ensign as our national flag?

Mr. Speaker, hon. members will be interested to know that in my riding, 62 people answered that they were in favour of keeping the Canadian red ensign while 347 were in favour of other flags.
As a second question I asked them:
Do you think that the flag issue should have priority before the unemployment issue, the pension plan or the farm problem?
The results were as follows: 132 replied that the flag issue should be settled first, while 278 were in favour of the settlement of the unemployment issue, the farm problem and the adoption of the pension plan.
The third question I asked them was:
Supposing that you are in favour of a new flag, would you indicate below which one you prefer:
1.	Flag embodying the Canadian red ensign and the fleur-de-lis?
Seventeen were in favour of that design. I carry on:
2.	Flag embodying the Canadian red ensign, the maple leaf and the fleur-de-lis.
Seventy four were in favour of that flag design.
The third design I suggested was a flag with three maple leaves. Two hundred people of my riding were in favour of the three maple leaf design.
As a last question, I suggested a flag with one maple leaf only. Only hundred and forty one of my electors were in favour of that design.
Mr. Speaker, in adding together those who were in favour of a flag design other than that submitted by the Prime Minister, we reach a total of 294, whereas those who chose the three maple leaf flag number only 200.
But at the beginning of June, I decided to make another poll. May I read the letter I sent to 1,751 citizens, in which I asked them to enlighten me on the choice of a Canadian flag. I said to them:
Dear Friend:
Once more, I take the liberty to ask your cooperation and I submit a few questions on the flag issue. I am sure you will rush your reply, and I wish to thank you in advance for your valuable assistance.
As you certainly know, the project of the Prime Minister, Mr. Pearson, is to officially establish, as a Canadian flag, a flag composed of three maple leaves on one stem, and to decree that the union jack be flown as a symbol of Canadian membership in the commonwealth of nations and our allegiance to the crown.
He also intends to decree that "O Canada" be considered as the national anthem and ''God Save the Queen" as the royal anthem.
In practice, the adoption of Mr. Pearson's project would mean that we would have two flags and two national anthems. I would like to have your point of view on this question and I would ask
Canadian Flag
you to fill in the enclosed questionnaire and to return it to me as soon as possible.
Thanking you for your usual co-operation.
I remain.
Yours truly,
Theo. Ricard, M.P.
St. Hyacinthe-Bagot
The questionnaire included four questions, the first of which read as follows:
Are you in favour of two flags?
464 answered: No, while only 8 favoured two flags.
The second question was the following:
Are you in favour of only one flag?
490 constituents answered: Yes, while only 8 answered: No.
The third question was:
Do you feel that rather than to have two flags, it would be better to maintain what we have at present?
273 constituents gave their preference to the status quo, while 76 answered: No. The fourth question was the following:
Do you feel it would be preferable to have a referendum on that matter?
Mr. Speaker, it is worthy of notice that 216 replied in the affirmative and 155 in the negative.
Mr. Speaker, on the basis of the information I obtained following those two soundings of opinion I have taken the attitude that a referendum, a plebiscite or a popular consultation should be held on the flag issue. I feel I have carried out the mandate my constituents have given me not only on the flag issue but on all other questions of national interest.
Mr. Speaker, to give an idea of the interest shown by the Canadian people in the holding of a referendum, I should like to quote an article which appeared in the Oshawa Times
and which reads as follows:

"Taxes and jobs main topics for Canadians". I should like to read a few extracts from this article:
"If you were writing to your member of parliament in Ottawa about the things you think parliament should do, what would you suggest?"
A similar question was asked in the United States recently and what came to the top there was taxes, as well as the civil rights bill. Medicare was cited in third place but only 2 per cent of Canadians mentioned need for a good medical plan and for more hospitals.
We read among the things judged as most important by the people across Canada that taxes are what Canadians would like to see reduced first. Then comes unemployment; the

Canadian Flag
encouragement of more industry; and then, fourth, a revised unemployment insurance fund. Then finally what is interesting people and is in the minds of the people is the cost of living.

This goes to show, Mr. Speaker, that there are several measures to which the house could have given serious consideration before dealing with the flag issue.
To repeat what others have said before me, people are anxious to see that matter settled but, at the same time, they are aware that any hasty and irresponsible action could inflict wounds on our national unity which would take generations to heal.
Mr. Speaker, I was greatly amused to hear the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Marcoux) and the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Frenette) suggest that a motion for closure be passed to put an end to this debate.
However, a few moments before making that suggestion, both members-I am sorry neither one is here at present-had made much of the fact that they were in favour of a distinctive national flag.
By suggesting the passage of a motion for closure, those two members actually recommended the adoption of the three leaf flag as the first national flag, and that the flag of a foreign country, that is, the union jack, be given an official status in the statutes of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, during their private conversation, my Liberal friends from the province of Quebec suggest that the second part of the resolution is merely a gilded pill to have a distinctive national flag adopted, and they claim that after a while, the second part of the resolution would be forgotten and the union jack would no longer be flown in our country.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I should like to dispute the validity of that suggestion of our friends opposite, because I do not believe that by decreeing and entering into Canada's statutes that a certain flag will be the official flag we will force people to forget another flag. You and I-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. May I interrupt the hon. member to remind him that the resolution he referred to is not under consideration at this time. By the same token, I take the liberty of reminding him that we are now considering the subamendment presented by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill).

I thank you, Mr. Speaker. I thought I could follow in the footsteps of the previous speakers.
But, since you are responsible for maintaining order in the house, I have no choice but to accept your ruling, which I do willingly and with respect for the authority you represent in this chamber.
I would now like to give the views of some of our best editorial writers on the flag issue.
But before doing that, Mr. Speaker, like my colleague from Rimouski (Mr. Ouellet), I would like to call on the good will of the members of the House of Commons to reach a final understanding on this burning question.
You will admit, Mr. Speaker, that we have now reached a decisive turn. I do not believe that this national flag issue can be settled without a compromise which would be acceptable by all the parties concerned.
I should like again to commend my colleagues from the other English speaking provinces for the dignity with which they tackled the problem. Each and all of them have risen in the house and expressed the views of their constituents. And they added that they were ready to accept a compromise. I think, Mr. Speaker, that they could not show better cooperation.
I should like to set out this courageous attitude as an example to my friends opposite, and particularly to those from the province of Quebec, so as to prompt them to stand up and to express their views on this matter. Really, I cannot see how they could feel free not to avail themselves of this opportunity to express their point of view as well as that of their constituents.
I pity them much more than I blame them for being bound in such a way by party discipline. Before resuming my seat, I should like to urge them once more to tell the House of Commons about the views of their fellow citizens.
It is important that they participate objectively in the discussion in the same way as we are now doing in an effort to solve this problem. It must not be forgotten that this is a problem that concerns them as much as us.
I am conscious that the official opposition has a very important role in this house. It must be recognized that we have fulfilled this responsibility to the best of our ability and that, in so doing, we have surely rendered the people a service, because if the official opposition had not drawn the attention of the house and of the Canadian people generally to this question of the flags, since the Prime Minister plans to have two, it could, I repeat,

Business of the House
have caused deep wounds to Canadian unity.
I will close my remarks by repeating that I favour a distinctive national flag and that we should all take steps to ensure that this problem is settled in the most agreeable and friendly way possible, in order that national unity, instead of being jeopardized, may be consolidated and this is the wish of all of us on this side of the house.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to speak on our loyalties, our unity and our heritage of the past. I want to bring to mind that over the years we have had a cross on our flag that goes back to the crucifixion, the cross that was put there by the English in honour of their patron saint, St. George, who was a Macedonian. The cross of St. Andrew was placed on the flag by the Scots in memory of their patron saint, St. Andrew, who was a Jew and a disciple of Christ. There is also the third cross, the cross of St. Patrick which was added at a later date. St. Patrick, of course, was a Scotsman who was educated in France and then became the patron saint of Ireland.
I also want to direct the attention of the house to the fact that over the years of early history England was invaded time after time by the Scandinavians and the same thing was also happening in Europe. The Scandinavians invaded Europe and established a province in the northern part of France called Normandy. These same Normans were very closely related to the Normans who had remained in England after the Scandinavian invasions prior to 1066.
Then William the Conqueror invaded England and defeated Harold at the battle of Hastings, in which Harold lost his life. It is also interesting to note that Harold's mother was a Scandinavian. Some people will say: Why go back into history? I see some members are smiling. I say to you that if you have no love for your traditions and are ashamed of your past there is something wrong with you and you have something you want to cover up. I for one do not want to cover up the history of Canada and I am going to relate it.
William the Conqueror invaded England and conquered that land. He pillaged and laid waste the land and for 100 miles there was neither a house nor a person left. He brought with him from France the Latin
touch not only in politics but in religion, and in the feudal system which he brought to England and established there. That was the last Scandinavian invasion of England, and I think this is an important part of history when we consider it was this man who stopped any further Scandinavian invasions.
As a matter of fact, he laid the cornerstone of the England we know today. He introduced the feudal system. He was a pretty smart man in a great many ways because he set up the barons and knights on the one side, and then had the English doing the work as serfs on the other. But he did not trust the barons and knights and he also appointed sheriffs. He had two bodies, one to watch over the barons and the knights and another whose members went around making secret investigations. He was a smart man.
I also wish to point out that it was from these same Normans that Magna Carta came. As a lawyer, Mr. Speaker, you will recognize that this is the cornerstone of democracy wherever it is found in the world. I say to all members and to the people of Canada generally, what a tradition we have got. William the Conqueror introduced the French language into England. It was used in court, it was used by the gentry and together with Latin it was used by the church. It was the language of politics and political science in that day, while English was the language of the serfs. The combination of those languages, Mr. Speaker, resulted in a common language, the English language of today, the greatest language in the world.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker.
